sourceScope: Existing teaching-reading glosses, examples and CC-CEDICT senses. Other readings remain separate in Information.

entries.explanation: When you need a moment to catch your breath, think of 休. It means stopping what you’re doing for a while and giving yourself a rest. You’ll often meet it in 休息 (xiūxi), meaning ‘to rest’—an everyday way to talk about pausing and relaxing.
Imagine a tree standing in front of you. 木 can refer to the tree itself or to the wood it gives us. In 木头 (mùtou), we’re talking about wood as a material—the kind you might use to make a table.
If you’re thirsty, 水 is the water you want to drink. It’s also the water you pour into a glass or see flowing in a river. In 喝水 (hē shuǐ), 喝 means ‘drink’, so the whole phrase means ‘drink water’.

When something is good, or you’re doing well, 好 is a word you’ll reach for often. In the greeting 你好 (nǐ hǎo), the whole expression simply means ‘hello’. Notice the tone here: hǎo. The reading hào has a different meaning, which you can explore in Information.
Start with a person—someone like you or me. 人 can refer to one person or to people more generally; the surrounding words tell you which. In 人们 (rénmen), you’re talking about people as a group.

Think of flames giving off heat and light: that’s 火. Now put it next to 山, ‘mountain’, in 火山 (huǒshān). The whole word means ‘volcano’—a memorable way to connect the two characters without treating every Chinese word as a literal translation.

Picture a mountain rising above the land around it. That’s the everyday idea of 山. In 高山 (gāoshān), 高 adds ‘high’, so you’re talking about a high mountain. Keep that landscape in mind when you meet 山 in other words.
Look up at the night sky and think ‘moon’: that’s one meaning of 月. You’ll also use 月 for a month when talking about dates. In 月亮 (yuèliang), the whole word means the moon you can see in the sky.

Think of the sun, then of one day passing. 日 connects with both ideas, and you’ll also meet it in calendar dates. In 今天是几月几日？, 几日 asks for the day of the month. The surrounding words help you choose the meaning.

Start with one thing, rather than two or three: that’s 一. In 一个 (yí gè), 一 tells you there is one item and 个 helps you count it. You’ll hear the tone change in this phrase, even though the dictionary reading is yī.

Use 不 when you want to say ‘not’ or make a negative statement. In 不是 (bú shì), you’re saying ‘is not’—for example, that something isn’t yours. Listen for bú before shì; the tone changes in speech, while the dictionary reading stays bù.
When you put something to use, 用 is the idea to remember. In 有用 (yǒuyòng), the whole word means ‘useful’: something has a use or can help you. Try connecting 用 with a tool or method you actually use.

definitions: Connects a description to a noun
entries.explanation: Think of 的 as a small connector between words. In 我的 (wǒ de), it links ‘I’ to something that belongs to me, giving you ‘my’ or ‘mine’. It can also connect a description to a noun, so read it together with the words around it.

definitions: Signals a change or new situation
entries.explanation: Think of 了 as a clue that something has happened or the situation has changed. In 我已经吃过饭了。, the speaker is telling you they have already eaten. It isn’t simply a past-tense ending: its meaning comes from the whole sentence.
